chapter_theme: The impermanence of youth (இளமை நிலையாமை): the sun's daily course and the calf grown old show that youth is passing, yet people do not take it in; the time to think of Siva and praise him is now, while life and youth remain.
structure_note: Verses on time's passing (177, 182, 184, 185) alternate with Tirumular's own voice: the aged man no longer desired (180) and the one who clings to the Lord's feet and saw him in his days (181, 186).

177.reading: Even seeing the sun that rose in the east run its course and fall in the west, eyeless people do not grasp it; even seeing a young calf become an old bull in a few days and fall, people of the wide world do not grasp it.
177.nuance: The two lines are built alike (விழக்கண்டும் தேறார்): the day and a life follow the same arc. விழியிலா (without eyes) is the blindness of those who see and do not understand.

178.reading: Many years have gone by, and none have taken the Father to themselves, entered and known him; though the long ages give still longer time, they do not know the flame of the lamp whose wick is raised.
178.nuance: தூண்டு விளக்கு (a lamp whose wick is pushed up to burn bright) is traditionally taken as the inner light, or the Lord within. The point stands either way: more time does not bring knowing.

179.reading: Youth wears away and is gone at last, and after one's power for hard deeds is spent; so think on and hold to Nandi of the spreading locks into which the Ganga leapt, while life is still in you.
179.nuance: The verb அற்ற (ended) runs through the first three lines: youth ended, strength ended, the Ganga's rush ended in his hair. The last line makes the urgency plain: உயிருள்ள போதே.

180.reading: Before, tender women desired me as the juice pressed from crushed sugarcane; to those bejewelled women with breasts like buds, I who was like sugarcane am now like the bitter kaanjiram fruit too.
180.nuance: The poet speaks of himself: the same man was cane and is now strychnine fruit (காஞ்சிரங்காய்) to the same women. The உம் in காயுமொத்தேன் may mean he was both in turn.

181.reading: Seeing the times called child, youth and old man pass, people still do not understand; I lie at the feet of the one who passed beyond the world and cut through the cosmos, and desire them still more.
181.nuance: ஞாலம் கடந்து அண்டம் ஊடறுத்தான் (who passed the world and pierced the cosmos) fits the tradition of Siva as the boundless column of fire. The verse turns from what others fail to see to the poet's own clinging.

182.reading: For those who rise in the morning, day after day evening falls and the life span passes; though that Lord is hard to hold, he gives joy to those who think of him fittingly.
182.nuance: சலவியன் is obscure: perhaps 'the changeful one', 'the one hard to approach' or 'the one who moves'. ஏல நினைப்பவர் may be those who think of him fittingly or those who think of him early.

183.reading: Five thick needles live in one bag; the five needles are a flying beast; when frost falls on the five needles, the needle bag itself flies off.
183.nuance: A riddle. The bag is commonly read as the body and the five needles as the five senses; பனித்தலைப் பட்டால் (when frost falls on the head) may be old age and grey hair. The four lines all begin பருவூசி, which may also play on பருவம் (season of life).

184.reading: People do not understand at all that the moon and the burning sun stand within and measure out the world; those bound for heaven and those bound by deeds alike are cut down at the counted thirty.
184.nuance: கண்ணதும் is read as the moon, the other eye of the sky; yogic readings make sun and moon the two breaths. எண்ணுறும் முப்பதில் (at the counted thirty) may be the thirty days of a month or a span of years; I can't fix it.

185.reading: Seeing the sixteen kalas joined and standing together, the base do not reflect; after harsh Death has put them in the pit of the womb, they fall into it again, their bewilderment not ending.
185.nuance: The sixteen kalas (ஈரெண் கலை) are the moon's sixteen digits, full only for a moment before waning; in yoga they have an inner sense as well. கருக்குழி (the womb pit) names rebirth.

186.reading: In the days you have, that youth may not pass in vain, praise him in song in the days you have; not knowing in the days I had what would be cast off, I stayed in the days I had and saw.
186.nuance: எய்திய நாளில் (in the days one has reached) opens every line. எறிவது (what is thrown or cast) is unclear: the body, youth, or Death's blow. The object of கண்டேன் (I saw) is left unsaid, taken as the Lord.

links.note: Both read the sun's daily course as a measure of passing life: the Naladiyar urges help to others before one's days run out, Tirumular faults those who see the sun set and do not understand.
In the Naladiyar Death uses the sun as a measure to eat one's days; in Tirumular the sun and moon measure out the world from within. Both make the heavenly lights the counters of a life.

The Naladiyar says not to put off good deeds because one is young; Tirumular says to hold to Nandi while life lasts, since youth and strength wear away. The urgency is the same, the act urged differs.
The Naladiyar warns men not to desire a woman who will one day stoop over a staff; Tirumular turns the lesson on the man, who was cane to women and is now bitter fruit.

source_issues: 177 line 1 reads கிழக்கெழுந்த் தோடிய, with a stray pulli on த்; probably கிழக்கெழுந்தோடிய.
182 line 4 reads நினைப்பவர்ககு, a misprint for நினைப்பவர்க்கு.
